description: We’re building MARS Twinsight, a Mars exploration game inspired by AI4Mars imagery and MEDA instrument concepts. Players collect trustworthy science, manage resources, and choose an outpost site. We welcome teammates interested in space, games, and science education. Looking for JavaScript/Three.js developers, UI/UX designers, GIS/data researchers, storytellers, and playtesters. Join us to make planetary science playable.
summary:
MARS Twinsight is an interactive Mars exploration game that helps players understand how scientific evidence shapes mission decisions. Players operate a rover, prepare virtual instruments, collect trustworthy readings, survey terrain, compare routes, and recommend an outpost location.

The project addresses the challenge of making Mars exploration and environmental information understandable through hands-on gameplay. Its landscape draws visual inspiration from AI4Mars imagery, while instrument mechanics follow concepts from the Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer (MEDA) specification. Terrain geometry and environmental readings are clearly labeled as simulated.

Its distinctive mechanic rewards players for checking data quality rather than simply collecting more data. Changing conditions, science objectives, and resource tradeoffs encourage replay. MARS Twinsight aims to make planetary science accessible while developing curiosity, critical thinking, and evidence-based reasoning.
details:
What it does and how it works

MARS Twinsight places players inside a first-person rover research mission. They choose one of three science objectives: Thermal Transect, Wind Watch, or Pressure Watch.

Players prepare their instruments before collecting readings. Depending on the instrument, they must check conditions such as rover movement, sensor visibility, shadows, antenna activity, and wind-boom configuration. Unsuitable readings are rejected with an explanation, helping players understand why data quality matters.

The mission continues through four research stops where players survey terrain, review environmental conditions, and document an outcrop. New terrain evidence changes the modeled crossing cost, prompting players to reconsider their routes. They then recommend an outpost and return to base.

Changing simulated conditions affect visibility, driving speed, and energy consumption. Scores reward trusted science, completed research, resource management, and optional objectives. Players can retry the same sol—a Martian day—or explore another scenario.

Benefits and intended impact

The project turns scientific concepts into decisions players can experience. It encourages them to distinguish trustworthy evidence from unsuitable readings, recognize uncertainty, and explain tradeoffs between distance, energy, and research opportunities.

The intended audience includes students, beginning programmers, GIS learners, and informal science visitors. Its educational impact is an intended outcome; learning gains have not yet been measured.

Tools and technologies

  • JavaScript, HTML, and CSS: Gameplay, interface, controls, and responsive layouts.
  • Three.js and WebGL 2: Interactive terrain, rover viewpoint, lighting, and visual overlays.
  • Vite: Frontend development and production builds.
  • Node.js and Express: Local application server and mission API.
  • SQLite and browser localStorage: Mission saves, preferences, and completed-run history.
  • Python: Optional data-preparation scripts and browser-test automation.
  • Node’s test runner, Playwright, and Chrome: Logic, mission-flow, and responsive-interface verification.

The game runs in a compatible browser without specialized scientific hardware.

Creative approach

The central gameplay idea is collecting science you can trust. Instrument preparation becomes a puzzle, while the digital twin connects observations to an evolving mission model. Players see how new evidence can change a plan rather than merely filling a checklist.

Factors considered

Development considered scientific transparency, readable typography, keyboard and touch controls, resource balancing, replay value, local persistence, and clear feedback. AI4Mars imagery and the MEDA specification provide reference material, while the game explicitly distinguishes its authored simulation from measured Mars conditions.
